title: Speed first: make every hook call cheap

short.lead: I propose five measured steps to cut the time every tool call spends in hooks; you pick how far to go and approve one option.
short.hint: Tap a step to see it.
items: A small timing script replays real Write and Bash hook calls and prints milliseconds per call. The baseline is saved.

items.alt: A Write call goes through the hooks and comes out as a millisecond number
items.caption: Step 1: a number to beat.

items: Load only what an event needs
Each hook stops importing all 7 parts before it looks at the event name. Measured today: 66 ms against 14 ms for bare Python.

items.alt: Nine slow hook boxes become nine light ones
items.caption: Step 2: less work per process.

items: The checks before a Write run in one process, and the ones after in another. A Bash call goes from 6 processes to 2.
The commit gate stops making 5 network reads on every Write (748 ms measured).

items.alt: Five network reads become one cache lookup
items.caption: Step 4: no repeat network reads.

items: A correctness fix on the same path: parallel hooks currently lose log lines.
A line in the decisions log.
Pick an option for each question, then send the approval line.

changes: A script under tools/ runs the real hooks against a scratch repo and prints milliseconds per call, for a Write and for a Bash call.
Speed was measured by hand, once, by reviewers.
One command that repeats the measurement.
You see the before and after numbers.
Load per event, not all at once.
Only the parts the event needs
hook.py maps each event to the module that handles it and imports only that one. Adding an event gets easier too: today it takes 6 edits.
The same handlers run in the same order inside one process per phase. Failure rules stay: guard still fails closed.
Labels are remembered for 60 seconds and cleared when the hook records a label change itself.
Trims only when the file grows past a limit.
No check is removed or weakened. verify.py must still pass in full. The guard holes stay for the later guard phase, as you asked.
choices: scope
How far should the speed work go?
A
Steps 1 to 5: measure, load less, merge, cache labels, fix the log
These are the measured costs, and the merge step builds on the load step.
B
Only steps 1, 2 and 4
Smallest change. Leaves 9 processes per Write, so most of the saving stays.
A reaches the biggest costs, and every step is measured before and after.
judge
The model call at the end of every reply: change it?
A
Run it only when a roadblock phrase is found
Removes a paid call and up to 22 seconds from most replies. A reply with no phrase is no longer judged.

choices.alt: Judge call every reply versus only on a phrase
choices.caption: Option A.

choices: B
Leave it as it is
No behaviour change, and the cost stays.
C
Make it opt-in, off by default
Fastest, but the judge never runs unless you switch it on.
A keeps the judge for the cases it was written for. It changes what is checked, which is why you choose.
tests
Speed up the test suite in this round too?
A
No, leave it for the code-quality phase
You asked for hook speed first, then code quality. The suite fix is a per-case runner, which is a quality job.
B
Yes, include the lazy fixture setup (1.1 s per part) now
Quick win, but it touches checks/common.py before the quality phase.
A keeps this round to hook speed.

wrapup.summary: Five steps that make the hooks cheaper per call, each measured before and after, with every check kept.
wrapup.changing: hook.py, hooks.json, the commit gate's label reads, the hook log, and a new timing script under tools/. No check is removed.
wrapup.blocking: Your three choices under Your choices, and the approval line.
wrapup.next: After you approve, the work is planned in a build plan with one issue per step, then built on a branch and measured.
